opus-5.5.text:
No, I don't think it will take a hundred years. The comparison with cars in the 1880s is more about where we are on the curve than how long the curve is. When Benz built his first car, it was this fragile, expensive thing that broke down constantly, and most people thought horses were simply better. That's roughly where general-purpose robots are today: impressive demos, but not yet reliable or cheap enough to change daily life.

But the pace of iteration is completely different now. Cars needed decades because everything had to be invented at once: roads, gas stations, manufacturing methods, even the idea of a driver's license. For robots, a lot of that infrastructure already exists. We have mature supply chains for motors, batteries, and sensors, largely thanks to phones and electric vehicles. We have massive compute. And most importantly, we have learning-based methods that let robots improve from data instead of hand-engineering every behavior.

So my rough guess is that we'll see robots become genuinely practical in specific settings, like factories, warehouses, and some service jobs, within the next five to ten years. A truly general home robot that can fold your laundry, cook, and tidy up reliably might take longer, maybe ten to twenty years, because homes are messy and unpredictable, and the bar for safety and reliability is very high.

The real bottleneck isn't hardware anymore. It's data and generalization: getting robots to handle the long tail of situations they've never seen. Once we crack that, and I think we're making real progress, things could move much faster than people expect. Like the Model T moment for cars, there will probably be a point where cost and capability cross a threshold, and adoption suddenly takes off.

r001.rationale: The response says robots can develop faster because iteration is quicker, supporting infrastructure and component supply chains already exist, and learning-based methods can improve behavior from data.

fable-5.1.text:
No, I don't think it'll take a hundred years, and I want to be careful about how that car analogy gets used. The point of the comparison isn't the timeline, it's the shape of the curve. In the 1880s you had cars that technically worked but were expensive, unreliable, and nobody knew what they were for. People looked at them and thought "this is a toy for rich hobbyists." Then roads, fuel infrastructure, mass production, and a clear use case all showed up, and within a few decades they reshaped cities. The lesson is that the gap between "a demo that works" and "something ordinary people depend on" is usually about the surrounding system, not the core machine.

What's different now is that the surrounding system is building much faster. We already have the compute, the sensors are cheap, the supply chain for actuators and batteries exists because of phones and electric vehicles, and the learning methods are improving on a scale of months rather than decades. So the thing that took cars forty or fifty years, I'd expect to see compressed into something like ten to fifteen for a lot of practical tasks.

But I'd also push back on the framing of "practical" as one moment. Robots are already practical in warehouses and factories. The question people really mean is "when will a robot do useful work in my home or in an unstructured environment." That's where I think we're genuinely still early. Manipulation in messy spaces is hard, reliability requirements are brutal, and a robot that fails one time in a hundred is not something you'd let near your kitchen. So my honest answer is: not a hundred years, probably not even twenty for the first really useful general-purpose ones, but the last mile of reliability is going to feel slower than the demos suggest.

r001.rationale: The response cites existing compute, cheaper sensors, established actuator and battery supply chains, and rapidly improving learning methods as reasons practical robots may arrive much sooner than a century.

astra-6.text:
No, I don’t think it will take another hundred years. The comparison with cars in the 1880s is about the stage of development, not the timeline. You can see the potential, but there’s still a gap between a compelling demonstration and something people can use reliably every day.

Robots can become practical in specific tasks before they become general-purpose. If a robot can do one useful job consistently, safely, and at a reasonable cost, that’s already practical. A robot that can walk into any home and do everything you ask is a much harder problem. So I’d expect progress task by task, rather than one moment when all robots suddenly become useful.

r001.rationale: The response rejects a hundred-year wait and describes practical progress task by task, but it does not identify advancing technology as the reason.
